After the tenders have been opened, any member of this House can obtain them on a motion for papers, and therefore I cannot see why the officials who open them should not open them in public or read out the names of the tenders and their prices. This does not oblige the government to accept the lowest tender, if good and sufficient reasons can be given for not doing so. As the tenders are for public works in which the whole public are interested, I think it is the duty of any government to give the public all. the information it can to show that it is doing what is right and proper and in the interest of the people. I have no desire to make this a party matter. I am making this suggestion entirely in the interest of the public. For years it has been the policy of the government-I do not say this government or its predecessors-to ask for tenders in two different ways. For large amounts they have advertised for tenders in the newspapers, and for smaller amounts they have simply written letters to half a dozen of their friends throughout the country, asking for prices for what they require. I claim that that is unfair to the people. I contend that everything over a certain amount, say $2,000, should be made a matter of public tender, by advertisement in the newspapers ; and if the tenders are opened in public, I am satisfied that an enormous amount of money will be saved to the people. Moreover, that will give the people of this country confidence in the ministers administering their departments. I simply appeal again to the government this year to accept this resolution. Also because we have a new House. We have now 80 or 90 members who were not here last year, and I ask them to consider this matter, not in a party spirit, but in the public interest. speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: I am sure that no member on this side of the House can yield anything to my hon. friend in his desire that, in the opening of tenders, every possible precaution should be taken to safeguard the public interest. As my hon. friend has said, the practice in the past has been to put tenders under lock and key, as soon as received, so that there could be no reasonable possibility of their being tampered with. The practice also has been to have the tenders opened by officials of the department and the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer unless there were some good reasons-such as his failure to give satisfaction in previous contracts or his financial inability-for submitting the matter to the Governor in Council for consideration as to whether or not the lowest tender was the best offer. As there has been some consideration given the question of the reception of tenders, both on the part of members of the opposition and members supporting the government, as well as by the government themselves, it was thought well to frame a new regulation which would lay down a rule applicable to all the departments. _ In doing this the government had to take into consideration the circumstances, more especially in regard to the Intercolonial Railway, whose head working office is at Moncton where tenders for supplies of various kinds are necessarily received. Had it not been for the fact that in the past it has always been considered desirable that tenders for supplies for the Intercolonial Railway should be received at Moncton, the rule would have been adopted that in every case tenders should be opened in the presence of the minister and his deputy or, in case of the unavoidable absence of the minister, then by the principal official of his department; but in the case of tenders received at Moncton it would not be possible for the minister to be present.
They could be opened by the officials.
Yes, they could be opened by three officials if there be any magic in having three instead of two. Had the regulation said three, by hon. friend would have said four.
Two could open them at Aloncton even according to your regulation.

Let me read the regulations and ask hon. members if they do not think it is sufficient to safeguard the public interest;-
Where tenders are called for by any department of the government, they shall be addressed to the officer of the department specified in the notice calling for tenders. The notice should say specially that the tenders shall he under seal and indorsed : ' tender for such and such work and supplies.' When received the tenders shall be stamped by the official to whom addressed, with the date and hour of receipt, and placed under lock and key until the day appointed for opening them. _ They shall be opened in the presence of the minister of the department calling for tenders and one of the principal officers of the department designated by the minister or, in the absence of the minister, in cases where it is not convenient for him to be present they shall he opened by two officials of the department designated by -the minister. When opened they shall he initialled by both officers opening them. In all cases where the minister oan reasonably be present, he must take part in the opening of the tenders and there must be one of the principal officers of the department present. And in. every case the tenders, when opened, must be initialled both by tbe minister and bis deputy. In cases where the minister cannot he present then it will he necessary for him to provide some official to take his place and he shall designate the official.
What virtue is there in the minister being present ?

The minister has the responsibility of his department and it is his duty to see what the tenders are when they are opened. I would hesitate to cast off the responsibility which the duties of my office place upon me, and throw that entirely upon one of my officials. It does seem to me that in providing that the minister shall be present and that the deputy minister- who occupies a position of great responsibility and almost complete independence -should take part in the opening of the tenders, we have a reasonable safeguard.
Does the minister think that my hon. friend's resolution would do away with the reception of tenders at Moncton for Intercolonial Railway supplies?

No; it does not, and that is the reason why the regulation provides that, where it is not convenient for this course to be adopted, the minister may designate two officials, and that provision is intended to apply to tenders received at Moncton. It seems to me that the only material provision in the motion which is not in the regulation is that all tenders shall be opened in the presence of the persons tendering. In other words that before the tenders are opened, notice shall be given all contractors so that they shall be present.
Mr. 3. D. REID. I say that they may be present if they so desire.
Then they must be notified of the time and place for opening the tenders.
You can put that in the advertisement.
The advertisement states that tenders will be received up to a certain day and hour.
And opened on a certain day and at a certain hour.
No, the notice does not say that.
It could say it and ought to.
The motion provides that.

Of coursd I understand that in order to carry out the idea of my hon. friend it would be necessary to give to the tenderers some notice so that they could be present when the tenders were opened. Apart from the inconvenience of that course, it is not desirable in the public interest that the public or the contractors should be present at the opening of tenders. My hon. friend has said that this course is adopted in the United States.^ His argument would have been stronger if he had been able to show that in any British country, in Great Britain or in any province of Canada, such a course had been adopted. My hon. friend knows that the course which has been pursued during the last ten years is the course which has been pursued during the whole 41 years of confederation.
No.
My hon. friend must be aware that the public have never been asked to be present at the opening of tenders in connection with any of the departments of- this government since confederation.
From the investigations that have taken place it would seem to be necessary.

I will discuss that in a few moments with my hon. friend. My hon friend has not been able to show that in Canada or in any province of Canada which has been under the control of either Liberals or Conservatives, it has ever been found desirable to adopt the course which he suggests, and it is a fair argument to raise before we entirely change the policy established in respect to both Dominion and provincial contracts, that my hon. friend has not been able to show either in the very full investigations which have taken place before the Public Accounts Committee or in



*
any other place that any minister of the Crown or any official of the Crown who has taken part with him in the opening of tenders _ has been untrue to the trust reposed in him by tampering with the tenders.
What about the timber limits ?

It has not been shown either in respect to tenders for timber limits or for lands of any kind or in respect to contracts for public works, that a minister or an official selected by him to be present at the opening of tenders has ever acted except in the public interest in the awarding of contracts. Take my own department. I shall take no credit for what I am about to say, but the rule is, and so far as I am able to learn it has always been strictly adhered to, that the tenders are received by the proper official, kept under seal, opened at the proper time and the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer.
By whom ?

By the minister and the deputy minister. Of course the minister does the actual awarding of the contracts and then the matter goes to council in the ordinary way. 1 do not pretend to say that in that respect we are any better than our predecessors, but I have never heard that under Conservative or Liberal rule anything has been done under the present system of receiving tenders by which the public has suffered and it would be a reflection it seems to me, and a very severe reflection upon the members of the government if the House were to hesitate to express its approval of the regulation which has been adopted. Before passing this regulation, very careful consideration was given to the matter, more especially by the Prime Minister and by the heads of the departments receiving the greater number of tenders and we were of the opinion that it would not be in the public interest to have the contractors present. It very often happens that there are two tenders for nearly equal amounts, and the nejft tender might be for an amount considerably greater than the amount of the two lowest tenders. If the tenders were opened in the presence of these contractors, they would see what the lowest tenders were and they would see that the next highest tender was perhaps a good many thousand dollars higher. They might easily put their heads together, have the lowest tenders withdraw, forfeiting their deposits, and thereby the minister would be compelled either to award the contract to the next lowest tenderer or to call for new tenders. Since I have been a minister I have seen some surprising differences in the amounts of tenders submitted for various public works. There was one case not long ago in which tenders were called for the erection of a public Mr. PUGSLEY.
building in a western city in which one of the tenders was very nearly 100 per cent higher than the lowest.
Issued by the same man?

No, not issued by the same man but by independent tenderers, who apparently had nothing whatever to do with each other, and if I had the tenders here I could cite numerous instances in which there has been a difference of many thousands of dollars between one or two of the lowest tenderers and some of those who might be called the higher tenderers. I have not sufficient faitli in human nature not to believe that when such a convenient opportunity was presented the contractors would in many instances combine together, have the lowest tenders withdrawn and thus compel the department to accept a very much higher tender or else invite new tenders, which would not be in the public interest. I think it much better to allow the officers of the department to deal with the tenders as it is ordinarily done, awarding the contract to the lowest tenderer, issuing an acceptance of the tender and taking the necessary steps for the entering into the contract so as to have the lowest tenderer bound before the public and the other contractors are made acquainted with the different tenders which have been received.
It does not seem to me that my hon. friend has shown to the House any good reason for making such a radical departure from the practice [DOT]which has been so long pursued without any objection, without any loss to the public, without any wrongdoing, so far as the public records show, or so far as my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) has been able to inform the House. I think the onus is upon my hon. friend of showing reasons which he has not adduced to the House before he asks us to enter upon such a radical departure. Therefore I feel it my duty to oppose the motion which my hon. friend has submitted.

Mr. Speaker. The principle which we are called upon to consecrate, appears to me to be a very important one, and I was surprised to hear the defence which has just fallen from the lips of my hon, friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) in regard to the regulation adopted by the government. That regulation, so far as I can see, does not meet the exigencies of the case at all. There is one thing absolutely certain, and that is a very general impression throughout the country, that there is something unfair in the manner in which tenders for contracts with the government are dealt with. There is not a man in any province of the Dominion, outside perhaps a limited circle of active politicians, who, if he were asked if public works in Canada were tendered for in a regular manner and

awarded to the lowest tenderer, circumstances being equal, would not burst out laughing in your face. That is the general impression. That general impression, I would add, prevents a great number of the very best class of contractors from tendering. There are men who are eminently capable of executing our public works at a reasonable price, and would be content with a fair and just profit, who abstain from tendering because they share that general impression that it is absolutely useless to tender unless you have some pull with those who dispose of the contracts. There is no doubt about that whatever. There is not a member of this House who has not been able to satisfy himself of the existence of that widespread impression. Is it not necessary that we should dispel that impression? Does not this proposed resolution have for its purpose to dispel that impression, and to provide for the tendering and awarding of contracts under the safest possible circumstances, without in any way interfering with the exercise of the judgment of the responsible minister? I say it does. What does the regulation provide for? It says that when tenders are received they will be put under lock and key. But that is not a safeguard of much importance. The very worst frauds perpetrated in regard to tenders have been effected when the tenders were put under lock and key. This resolution provides for something totally different. Tenders have to be sealed and put away; the moment they are sealed and put away they cannot be touched until the authority who has to decide who will get the contract, is in a position to pronounce. It seems to me there is a great deal of difference between the two provisions.
My hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), twice, three times, more than four times, repeated the assertion that since confederation, neither in the federal or the provincial sphere, had anybody every heard of any contract or any tender being improperly handled. Now that was the statement of my hon. friend; and coming from a gentleman of his vast experience, four times repeated, I must say it surprised me not a little. While I do not attempt to give instances, I appeal to the experience of those who have been in politics for some time, no matter which party ruled, whether they have not heard of irregularities in the awarding of contracts and the handling of tenders. There is no doubt that there has been in this country, federally, provincially and municipally, a. crying abuse in this respect. That abuse exists to-day. In order to dispel the general impression I refer to, and to convince the public at large that that system is going to be done away with, so far as we can do it, seems to me this resolution is necessary, and would cure _ a very grave situation indeed. Then again,
7i
Mr. Speaker, is it not inportant, does it not carry out the idea that we hear expressed every day on the street, that the tenderers themselves, more than that, the public, but particularly the tenderers, should be able to be present when the tenders are opened? They have not a voice in the decision, that is done privately on the responsibility of the minister. But what could contribute to make the opening of tenders, the recording of these tenders, more. effective, more authentic, so that no doubt could exist, than the right of the public, convened under the advertisement which invited tenderers, to be present, and for the tenderers themselves, whose interests after all deserve some consideration, who have gone to some trouble in making calculations and financial arrangements, to be present when these tenders are opened, in order that all may know what those tenders are? My hon. friend has supposed an extreme case, where there may be some low tenderers and some higher, and the lower ones might be eliminated, and, if you please, their deposit forfeited, in order that the highest tenderer should remain. I would be prepared to say that for my part I would take the risk, and we are all prepared to take the risk, of such an improbable possibility. As regards Great Britain, the mover of this resolution has shown that the custom is carried out. It is very generally carried out in the United States. But every one knows that in England the greatest publicity surrounds the opening of tenders for all public works. In England, as I have stated time and again, in this House, all supplies wanted by the government are invited by tender the greatest publicity is given to the tenders received, and I am perfectly convinced that if we refer to the regulations which govern the awarding of tenders followed by the government in England, we will see that there is just the same publicity that we advocate here.
I think not.

I believe so. At any rate. I am prepared to establish that there is a very different publicity in England surrounding the giving of contracts than what we find -here. But we are not dealing with England, we are dealing with our own country, and with conditions that we know to exist here; we are dealing with an impression firmly established in the entire nation that irregularities exist in regard to tenders and contracts. You cannot meet a contractor on the street, you cannot meet a man who takes any interest in public matters, who, if you put to him the question, will not answer :	Why, everybody knows
that this is a matter of favour. That is the impression. How can we efface it? Bv providing such a rule as this, and I have shown why I think it is important that such a rule should be adopted. We are

endeavouring to reform our public service, we are endeavouring to improve the administration generally. This is a crucial matter, and I have great pleasure in supporting the proposed resolution.

If I might offer a word or two on the resolution, I would say that, judging from the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Monk), his complaint, if he has one, against the regulation which has just been made by order in council in respect to the opening of tenders, is that greater publicity is not given in the first place, and in the second place, that there is some suspicion throughout the country of wrong-doing in regard to the system of dealing with tenders. I point out in the nrst place that whether sufficient publicity is given or not by way of advertisement, the motion of my hon. friend dqes not deal with that question. His motion deals only with the question of opening tenders. The only distinction, as far as I can see, between the regulation passed by order in council and the motion of my hon. friend is that the latter requires the presence of one more person when the tenders are opened than is called for in the regulation, and he gives to the tenderer the opportunity of being present when the tenders are opened. I deny that there is any very general misunderstanding or any very great suspicion throughout the country in regard to the manner in which the government deals with tenders, but I say that if any suspicion does exist it exists solely and only on account of the charges which were made in this House during the last two or three sessions, by lion, members opposite and in each case disapproved. Time and time again charges were made that tenders, in regard to timber in particular, were not fairly dealt with.
Insinuations.

Insinuations were made from day to day, investigation took place and in some of the investigations which did take place hon. members opposite, seeing the position in which they had landed themselves, had not even the courtesy or grace to continue the investigations to the conclusion to give officials against whom they had made insinuations an opportunity of clearing themselves. No charge has been established, though many charges were made, and if hon. gentlemen have induced the public to believe that there is wrongdoing in regard to the tendering system of Canada they should go the whole length and establish some of the wrong-doing. I am satisfied for my part that the regulation which has been passed in regard to tenders meets the case fairly and very fully. It provides for the presence of the minister and of one other chief official of the department when tenders are opened. My hon. friend's motion provides for another man. If two are not sufficient, would three be Mr. MONK.
any better? Why not four; why not five? Surely we must trust somebody in the conduct of public business, and if two high officials, or the minister and another high official of any department are entrusted with the duty of opening tenders, this House and, I think, this country will have confidence in their doing right on each occasion. There has never, in so far as I know, been a charge made that any tender has been tampered with. Tenders, when received, have been kept secretly and sacredly and the order in council provides that they shall be addressed to the proper officer of the department and that they shall be marked tenders for such and such work or for such and such supplies and that:
Whan received they shall be stamped by -the c-fficial to whom addressed with the day and hour of their receipt, and placed under lock and key until such time as it shall be found convenient for opening them.
I do not see any greater safeguard you can have unless there is so great a suspicion in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite that they will not trust two high officials of the department. For my part I think that the end will be served by the provision as contained in the order in council, and without discussing the question which has been so well answered by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, as to whether or not the parties tendering should be present when tenders are opened, I beg to move as an amendment to the motion:
That all the words after 'that ' be eliminated from the proposed motion and that the follow-mg be substituted therefor: The method of inviting, opening and considering tenders, as embodied in the order in council of January 18, 1909, is in the opinion of this House, a proper safeguard of the public interests.

Mr. Speaker, the question of opening tenders is a moot one in this House and has been again and again brought up for discussion. The objection to the plan of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugs-hy) as embodied in the order in council, I intend to deal with, and I also propose to say something with regard to some of the remarks of the hon. mover of the amendment to the resolution. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) seems to think that we ought to make a statement of some wrongs or frauds that have been perpetrated and prove them before we can introduce a resolution. Is it not sufficient to show that it is possible that a wrong may be done under the present system and if a remedy can be applied, is it not our duty to apply it? The minister proposes in the regulations that these tenders shall be opened by the minister and one of the officials of the department. It may be his private secretary. To my mind it is a most objectionable system for the minister to open tenders at all.

Under the constitution he has a right to superintend his department and if the regulations provide that a couple of officials shall open tenders, he can be there if he likes to see that the work is properly performed without an order in council or anything of the kind. What has been the system hitherto with regard to the opening of tenders? I presided over the Department of Railways and Canals for a number of years. The tenders were received, sealed and put into the safe. A certain time was provided at which they should be opened. They were opened by two of the officials named in the department for that purpose; that is to-day, the deputy head and the secretary of the department. If there was anything wrong in reference to the tenders, as to the time of their having been received, as to the amounts not totalling up, as to there being mistakes made or anything else, it was the duty of these two officials to report in writing to the minister and the minister was to be guided by the facts in reference to whether one tender or another should be accepted. In reference to the tenders down at Moncton, as my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) has stated, the system adopted by the British government is similar to that which we had in Moncton. There was a book provided in which the name of everything required from a box of tacks to a paint brush or an anchor was mentioned. This was sent broadcast from one end of the British empire to the other, and tenders were invited for the supply of these particular articles. These tenders were received and were awarded in every case to the lowest tenderer. If there -was a difference as to the quality of the article which it was proposed to supply it was left to an outside technical department to determine -whether one article was better than the other. A number of parties were asked to tender for a particular kind of work or a particular article. There was a list prepared. There was no difficulty at all about getting on the list; anybody could get on the list. Any responsible party who had the selling of these particular goods in the maritime provinces or in the province of Quebec could be put on the list. He tendered for a particular article. If one party was the lowest and the contract was awarded to that party by the officials at Moncton the officials had to give the reason for their action to the department here, the awarding of the contract had to be approved by the head of the department and a contract never was given until a sample of the article was sent to the technical branchy of McGill College in Montreal for examination. In this way, for instance, we would determine the quality of oil, or of steel. Then, on the report of the technical branch of McGill College the contract was awarded. In no case, when I was at the head of the department, was a contract awarded in any other way, and in no case were tenders received privately for
any work or orders given privately for any material. Everything was done by contract. The minister (Mr. Pugsley) objects to the public being parties to this

Will my hon. friend let me ask him a question ? I have been very much interested in the course which he says was pursued in the Railway Department, and unless the hon. gentleman informs me to the contrary I presume the same course is being pursued up to the present time, but will my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) tell me, if, during his day, the contractors were ever notified to be present at the opening of the tenders.

I shall deal with that. I do not know what the system is at the present day, but I know what it was in my day and I can state that except for a few trivial works on the St. Lawrence canals where it was impossible to give the work by contract, everything even to a paint brush was purchased by open competition while I was minister.
It was done on the canals then too.

That is the only course that should be pursued, and it is the course which the law requires this government to pursue but they evade what is embodied in the law. The Minister of Public Works says there has been no reason shown for a change in the system. Does he completely ignore the statements which have been made in this parliament during the last two or three sessions with reference to the granting of timber limits and the awarding of contracts ? Why the very fact that it is possible that such charges could be made is sufficient to call upon the government to ensure that nothing of the kind shall occur in the future. Did any one ever hear of any person objecting to publicity in the opening of tenders in Great Britain? Everything is above board there, except of course in certain cases where the specifications for a new type of torpedo boat or a new implement of warfare may be kept secret, but in regard to general matters such as the building of war ships and the building of everything else required by the British government, fancy a minister of the Crown there interfering in the awarding of contracts or thinking it was necessary for him to be present for the purpose of guaranteeing fair play. Why, Sir, in Great Britain there' is not a suspicion of fraud or a suspicion of anything but the fairest of play in the awarding of contracts. The Minister of Public Works deprecates adopting the American system and he says we should look to other places for example. Well, the American system was adopted because a suspicion had got abroad that there had not been fair play in the awarding of contracts and so the tenders were opened when the

tenderers were present. But, says the Minister of Public Works, the government may suffer ; two or three of those who are awarded contracts may combine, forfeit the securities deposited and get a higher price. Well, every contractor gives two securities and if the government find that a contractor deliberately refuses to perform his contract the remedy is in their own hands.
The hon. gentleman misunderstood what I said. I did not say they might combine together after they had entered into the contract, I said they might do so before the contract was actually signed.
How could they combine after they had entered into the contract ?
That, is exactly what my hon. friend said.
I couid mean nothing else than that they might combine before entering into the contract. Will that satisfy my hon. friend ?
Did not the hon. gentleman say that in addition to the deposit there would be a guarantee in the security that would have to be given when they entered into the contract ?

What I referred to was the deposit made by the party who was tendering for the contract. He could be made to forfeit that and not only that but he has to give the names of two securities who are satisfactory to the government for the due performance of his contract. But, independent of all this, suppose Jie does not forfeit his deposit or suppose the government does not proceed against the securities, cannot the minister say to that man who defaults :	You had a chance, you
contracted to do that work within a certain time, you refuse to fulfil it, I will have nothing to do with you and I will never give you a contract again. Therefore, there is a responsibility on the contractor greater even than his deposit and greater than the two securities which he gives. Any idea of combination before entering into the contract is something the minister need not consider at all because there is no probability of it. In order to secure honest dealing, at least what the contractors consider honest dealing with the department, it is but fair to them that they should have an opportunity to be present when Jlie contract is opened and there can be no possible objection to that on any grounds. The minister says there is no necessity for it. Is he unaware that from one end of the country to the other this government is under suspicion. So far as I am concerned I state from my place in this House that while I was a member of the Conservative government I never knew of any wrong-doing being perpetrated in reference to the awarding ' Mr. J. G. HAGGART.
of contracts. I state from my place that such a thing cannot be charged against any government of which I was a member. But, from one end of the country to the other that is not the opinion to-day.
It seems to be.

Your majority does not prove it, because there may be other things than the dealings of this government with contractors which affected the result. There is nevertheless a feeling throughout Canada that contracts have been awarded by this government to political hacks through favouritism or worse. What we ask is that there should be applied the remedy which is provided in most civilized countries. We ask that as is done by the American government there shall be the additional security of honesty in awarding contracts that the parties who tender shall be present. To that there can be no honest objection.

Mr. Speaker, what amused me was the position taken by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). He says there has been no charge made of wrong-doing in handling tenders or awarding contracts, and therefore there is no reason for a change. But the hon. Minister of Public Works proposes a change himself. Therefore if the logic of the hon. member for South Wellington applied to the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid), it applied with equal force to the hon. Minister of Public Works. Why did the minister propose a change ? Why did the Governor in Council make a change? For better safety, presumably. Why for better safety ? Because there is either a suspicion or knowledge that tenders have not been properly opened, and contracts have not been properly awarded in the past. Therefore it does not look very well for the hon. member for South Wellington to play the part of a handy man and address such an argument to the House, because it is not in consonance with the argument of the minister himself. What did the minister say in reference to this matter yesterday ?
I wAs going to suggest to my hon. friend that perhaps he will allow this motion to stand over, and, with your permission Mr. Speaker, and that of 'the hon. member, I will read to the House a regulation which has been passed by His Excellency the Governor General in Council, and (which I think my hon. friend will see, upon consideration, completely meets the ease.
The hon. minister is prepared to meet the case himself. What case ? The case the hon. member for Grenville desires to provide for. There is either a suspicion or knowledge of wrong-doing, and who proposes the change ? The government themselves, who are behind the scenes, and know whether there is or is not wrong-doing. This makes the case ten times strong-

er against them, because, if there was no wrong-doing or suspicion of wrong-doing, and if it was incapable of being established that there was wrong-doing, they would fight it out like men, and stand by what has been the practice and refuse to make a change. But is it a fact, as the hon. member for South Wellington says, that there have been no charges ? No charges ? Were not charges made over and over again in this House last session in connection with the awarding of timber limits ? No charges ? Circumstantial evidence, which in a murder case would be strong enough to hang a man ten times over, will not be accepted by the government. I venture to say that there is not amongst the hon. gentleman's own friends one in a hundred but honestly believes to-day that there was wrong-doing in connection with the awarding of those timber limits. Then we come to ordinary public contracts. Take the tenders for dredging. Why is it that all the dredging plant is to-day practically in the hands of reformers ? Why is it that the plant which was owned by Conservatives when the present government came to power, lay idle year after year until it was sold or transferred to reformers ? Because the owners of this plant had no opportunity of an honest deal to get a contract for dredging and were obliged to dispose of their plant.
Does my hon. friend know that ?

I was just about to say that I have been told it by the very men who had the plant. But after they sold it or went into an arrangement with a reformer, they had no difficulty in getting contracts. Will the Minister of Public Works pretend to tell the House that there was no collusion in that case in which it is alleged that a tender for dredging was changed from 50 cents to 55 cents a yard in order that there might be a rake-off of $35,000 ?
What case was that ?
The McAvity case.

If my hon. friend desires an answer, I will say that so far as I have been able to ascertain, so far as the records of the department show, and to the best of my knowledge and belief there was no alteration of the tender. There were two tenders put in, in answer to public advertisement, and the lowest tender *was accepted.

How does the hon. minister reconcile that statement with the statement of the contractor, who says he was willing to tender at 50 cents a yard, but by getting a friend to interfere on his behalf he got 55 cents a yard ?

I will answer that. I will say to my hon. friend that there appeared one morning in St. John what purported to be a certain solemn declaration which had been read by Mr. Hazen, the leader of the Conservative party, at a great political meeting in St. John, and that declaration did not purport to be signed by the party who professed to have made it. I know myself that it contained statements which were absolutely false, absolutely without foundation, and immediately an application was made to Mr. Hazen, who was the Attorney General of New Brunswick, to have the original of that declaration filed. Mr. Hazen replied that he had returned it to Mr. Mayes, and, although repeated requests have been made from time to time to have it produced so that it may be seen what was in the original, they have refused to produce it, and it has been concealed ever since the election.

That seems to me to be all beside the case. This man went to a certain individual who was known to be friendly to the government, and he got the contract at the larger figure. Who advised him to do so ? The minister himself who was awarding the contract. Is that creditable either to the minister or to the government ?
Does my hon. friend say that the Minister, of Public Works gave the advice ? Will the hon. member be good enough to repeat what he said ? I did not quite hear him.
I wish to make a correction in that respect.
Hear, hear.
It is rather amusing to hear the laugh come from the source it does. There is a good deal behind it that would be worth bringing out.
Make the correction.

I have as much right at any time to make a correction, as much right as any other member of this House. I was only mixing up two ministers ; but is it not a fact that the recommendation came from the very source that had the power to give the contract ?
What does that mean ?
According to the information disclosed in the public press, it did come from that source.
If I understand what my hon. friend means, I will say that he is entirely and absolutely in error.

In connection with that very case, there is the undeniable fact that the man who was willing to put in a tender at 50 cents a yard, got it increased to 55 cents a yard, and got it increased by virtue of the advice of the very individuals who had an opportunity to handle the tenders.

Does my hon. friend make the assertion that a tender was put in at 50 cents a yard and was subsequently changed to 55 cents ? In cases of this kind it is desirable that we should be accurate and that those who make statements should know what they are talking about. There have been falsehoods without number circulated with regard to the matter to which my hon. friend refers. They were scattered broadcast throughout Canada at the time of the election, and had not the shadow of a foundation of truth. So far as the records show, so far as I know, and so far as any statement has yet been made, no tender was altered from 50 cents to 55 cents a yard ; but there were two tenders put in, in answer to public advertisement, and one of those tenders was for 55 cents a yard.
Does the minister say that the same man who tendered for 50 cents did not afterward get 55 cents?

I will repeat what 1 have said. I have said that the man who tendered at 50 cents did not get 55 cents. The hon. gentleman is referring to entirely different tenders. In answer to a call by public advertisement, there were only two tenders submitted to the department-one for 55 cents and the other for either one dollar or one dollar and twenty five cents per cubic yard.
Was not that the same work that the same man tendered at 50 cents before?
On a previous occasion?
Yes.
I think it was.

I have what I regard as good ground because I saw the statement in the^ public press, and it was not denied by the minister. But w7ho gave the advice to Mr. McAvity to put in a higher tender? It was Mr. Pugsley himself.
Again the hon. gentleman is absolutely and entirely mistaken. I gave no such advice, and I venture to say that my hon. friend did not see in the newspapers that I gave any such advice.
I say emphatically, if my memory is correct, and I believe it is, that I did.
Your memory is mistaken.
My recollection is that the newspapers said that Mr. Pugsley advised Mr. Mayes as his solicitor.

My hon. friend makes a statement that it was I -who gave the advice to Mr. Mayes to raise his tender from 50 Mr. SPROULE.
cents to 55 cents. That statement is absolutely without foundation.
He did not say that. He said he saw it in the papers.
The hon. minister is indulging i:n a great deal of unnecessary special pleading and improper interference with my right to speak.
The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has the floor, but it is customary to allow7 a minister to make a personal explanation.

I rise to correct the statement made by my hon. friend. He said, if I heard him correctly, that he had seen it stated in a newspaper that I had advised Mr. Mayes to raise his tender from 50 cents to 55 cents.
No.
What did the hon. gentleman say?

What I intended to convey, and what I think I did say, was that the minister advised him to put in a tender at 55 cents per cubic yard for work which he had tendered to do the year before at 50 cents per cubic yard.
Let me say that I never gave any such advice and I defy the hon. gentleman ito produce ; any newspaper in which he saw that statement made.

Did not the Minister of Public Works see the solemn declaration of Mr. Mayes, and w'ill he say that Mr. Mayes does not there allege that the minister referred him to Mr. McAvity, and that Mr. McAvity advised him to increase the tender.
That is a very different matter. Settle one thing at a time. What does my hon. friend from Grey say to my correction?

I did not hear what the minister said the last time. I do not agree in the contention that there is no need of a change unless a case of wrong-doing is proven. I think it is quite sufficient to have a well-grounded suspicion of wrong-doing to justify the government or parliament in providing some remedy. But in this case there is more than suspicion because in case after case, submitted to this House last session, the facts were established over and over again. I am now referring to the dredging contracts. It is well known, at least in Ontario, that Conservatives who own dredging plants cannot get a government contract unless they pass their plant over to reformers or join in with reformers. But once they take in some prominent Reformer or friend of the government, they can get contracts and make

lots of money. How is it that the dredging business is so remunerative to-day, compared with ten or twelve years ago, if there be no wrong-doing? No one who knows anything, can fail to reach the conclusion that the reason the business is so remunerative to-day is because of wrong-doing and not because of the carrying out of a proper system of tender and contract. That is the impression all over the west, and it is well grounded, and it is high time we should have a change. Surely there can be no objection to those who tender being present when the tenders are opened. I can see strong reasons for some change that will inspire and restore public confidence and give the public some assurance that when a man tenders for timber limits or dredging or public works or anything else, he will be fairly and honestly dealt with.

When I heard the motion proposed by my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid) I was not surprised to find that it did not receive much sympathy from the government and I could appreciate the uneasiness of the members of the government over this attempt on the part of the opposition to take away from them what is practically their life's blood, by means of which they have been able to secure a . majority of seats in this House. This resolution is in principle one of the most important ever submitted to Parliament. It aims at the very crux of the corruption which is eating out the heart of the country and has done so much to lower public morality. Well may the cabinet ministers from the first minister down to the Minister of Public Works, look grave and concerned over this matter. It was certainly in very poor taste for the Minister of Public Works to defy public opinion as he has done, and to deny that there is in this motion a principle of public morality iwhifch it is the bounden duty of every minister, as well as every member of parliament and every honest, loyal Canadian citizen, to maintain and uphoid to the best of his ability.
I do not propose to repeat what has been said, but there are two questions to be dealt with in connection with the opening of tenders. There are two evils, with which the government is very familiar, which the right hon. the leader of the government knows right well are rampant, and which have led to the worst corruption and government mismanagement. What are they? One is the lack of protection against absolute secrecy from the time the tender leaves the hands of the party tendering until opened in the presence of some responsible minister or officer. I need not refer at length to the debate of last session upon the notorious timber deals, where tenders were opened by an officer now sitting in this House, opened in secret and in a manner which did not give confidence to the people who were tendering or to the people of this country and which did not work out for the conservation of the national assets of this country.
The next principle involved is that of the publicity and consequently the security of the dealings with the tender. I was surprised at the speciousness with which the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) attempted to evade that question. I can see no objection to tenders being opened in public. Surely the public moneys ought to be conserved, and surely when the public moneys have to be expended it is to the public interest that the lowest tenderer should get the work provided he is competent and that his and all other tenders are honestly and fairly dealt with. There is an aspect of this debate which is ludicrous in its incongruity and inconsistency. In the last election we saw an hon. gentleman from New Brunswick parading around the country promising works here, there and everywhere to anybody and everybody in order to obtain the support of that province for the government of which he was a minister. Is there any significance in the attitude taken by the Minister of Public Works now ? Does he see in this measure some means by which he will be less able to deliver the goods which he promised at that time? The speech of the hon. minister conveys the impression to my mind, and I am sure to the minds of the people generally, that what he desires is, not the security of the tender not the secrecy of the tender until it shall be opened in public, but a laxity of procedure and secrecy from the time the tender leaves the hands of the tenderer until it is proclaimed absolutely in the hands of a politician, a member of this House. I understand that the hon. gentleman did in a burst of righteous zeal, when his mind was in that state of exaltation from which we sometimes get the evanescence in this House, state that he had dispensed with the patronage system in his department. His speech in opposition to this motion possibly evidences the man-[DOT] ner in which he proposes to dispense with the patronage system in the Public Works Department, and I suppose that is about all the sincerity one can attach to the words of the Minister of Public Works, especially when he is on the stump.
The hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) objected very seriously to any suspicion being cast with reference to political interference with tenders. May I recount to the First Minister an incident which occurred during the last election with which he may be familiar as it has been brought to his attention ? The works of the Algoma Steel Company were closed down for lack of orders. Tenders were invited by

the National Transcontinental Railway Commission for some 40,000 tons of steel rails and the Algoma Steel Company, the Dominion Steel Company and the United States Steel Company were rival tenderers for this order. The tenders were in, supposedly sealed and secret, and they were to be opened on the first of September. The government candidate in West Algoma came to Ottawa, brazenly announcing that he was coming here to secure for the Algoma Steel Company as large an amount of that contract as they should receive. He was a new candidate and so was not as cautious as some of the others. The tenders were opened and the Algoma Company, most unjustly as we thought, got only one-third of the order. But that gentleman paraded all through the county boasting if he had not come to Ottawa and exercised his influence in respect to these secret tenders not a pound of these rails would have been awarded to the Algoma Company. The Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Graham) visited Sault Ste. Marie and when he appeared on the public platform I addressed an open letter to him asking him to give to the people of that county an affirmation or denial of these statements. The hon. gentleman said that he had not time to attend to it at that time. Are there other similar instances ? Yes, Sir. I have in my possession now a letter from a gentleman now occupying a seat on that side of the House asking in reference to vested interests in Northwest timber lands, whether the man who had the vested interests, namely, a license, was a Liberal or a Conservative, because that might make a great deal of difference, and if he was an active Conservative worker he might be able to get the land away from him. Hon. gentlemen opposite say there are no charges or suspicion of charges of political influence in the awarding of tenders. The administration of every department as revealed in the last two sessions reeks with it, and if the Minister of Public Works were to travel for a thousand years from end to end of this country he would not be able to satisfy the people of Canada that there is honesty, probity, secrecy and propriety in the opening of and dealing with tenders. It is just as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) says, the mercantile world bursts out laughing at you if you allege that this government deals honestly with tenders for public works. I come now to the question of the interest of members on the government side of this House in tenders. Two sessions ago I asked a question of the Prime Minister with reference to a member of his party who I believe as a member of parliament obtained contracts, which if he had obtained in his own name would have constituted a breach of the law, but to avoid that he incorporated himself, his wife, his cousins and his aunts into a cor-Mr. BOYCE.
poration called by his own name with the word ' limited ' after it. The right hon. gentleman when asked the question simply said that he was not aware whether the hon. gentleman referred to had any connection with the corporation to which I referred. That is another affair. You have the matter of the dredging contracts, to which my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has referred, and there you have a state of things most revolting. You have practically a state of things where certain dredging firms, in which members of parliament are largely interested, members, and ex-members and defeated candidates of the Liberal party, have formed a nice little ring by which they might know when tenders are to be asked for dredging ; and that one man writes out a tender for two, one man signs for another, the same tenders go in the envelope of another firm, and so on. Where is secrecy, and where is competition there ? The Minister of Public Works has had that brought to his attention, and he sneers at it.
Now just a word in regard to the principle involved in this motion. If the Minister of Public Works desires in any way to pose as being sincere, I see no reason whatever why he should not accept the principle of the motion. I see no reason why the right hon. the Prime Minister, who has secured the confidence of the country for another parliament, should not see in this motion a means of effecting the reform which I understand he has promised in this very matter of departmental administration. My right hon. friend said at Niagara Falls, when confronted with this state of things, that he himself was no saint. I sincerely hope that my right hon. friend, knowing the condition of affairs, as he must know it, will see in the acceptance of this motion by himself something which will redound to his credit, and something which he can claim as a fulfilment of the promise he made on the hustings. If such a resolution were carried and put into effect, what great sums of money would be saved to this country. But I fancy there is no danger of this resolution going into force, for the reason that this resolution is aimed at the very life of this government. What would become of the party heeler? What would become of the hanger-on? What would become of the man who is waiting for a tip, who provides the money for election campaigns, the man whose interest must be protected at all costs? What would become of him if all the tenders had to be kept sealed? Why, Sir, the principle of secrecy is as abhorrent to the members of this government, apparently, as it was to the Department of the Interior at the time of this nefarious timber limit deal that was exposed last session. Mr. Speaker, I unhesitatingly support this motion because I think that the principle of it is one which

will work excellent results for the stability of Canadian institutions.

Being one of the new members from the province of Ontario, I would not have ventured to address you to-day were it not that some reference has been made to dredging contracts. I come from a riding which is the home of a dredging and construction company, and perhaps you will pardon me if I say a few words with respect to this motion. The hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has said that if there was a feeling of insecurity in this country witli reference to the opening of tenders, it was a feeling which had been engendered by the action of the Conservative party, especially during the last session. Now, if that is so, there must be some reason for the change in the manner of opening tenders. If a change has been made in the manner of opening tenders by the Minister of Public Works, it must be because he, from an inward consciousness, believes it is necessary to do so, or because he believes that the Conservative party was justified in making the accusations they did. I desire to say from my seat in this House that I believe the Conservative party were justified in making the accusations they did last session. It has come to pass in this country that people believe that it is necessary to be a member of the Reform party, to be of the same political faith as this government, before you can secure a dredging contract from this government. In my own constituency, the North riding of Grey, as you all know, we have representing us in the local house the Hon. A. G. MacKay, leader of the Liberal opposition in the province of Ontario. It may be a coincidence, but it is so, that that gentleman is also president of the Owen Sound Dredging and Construction Company; it may be a coincidence that, although the assets of that company are worth anywhere from $100,000 to $200,000, he and the relatives of a late Liberal member in this House, own all the stock of that company except three shares of $300, and that these 3 shares consisting of $100 each are distributed nominally among three other persons for the sole purpose of constituting the necessary five in order to be incorporated as a dredging and construction company. That is the company about which there was so much examination in the Public Accounts Committee. We find that that company had obtained contracts from this government practically without any competition whatever; they obtained contracts from this government, as you know, by one consulting with the other, and the tenders, as you know, went into the envelope of one tenderer, and in that manner they were able to get these contracts. Then the Minister of Public Works, in order to alleviate somewhat the pressure of public opinion against
this government, changed that system to a system of letting contracts by t&nder. I understand that when contracts were subsequently let by tender, the figures were higher than they were during the time that contracts were let without tender.
Will my hon. friend allow me to correct him?
Order.
I wish to correct my hon. friend.
Order. He ought not to be interrupted.
It is customary for an hon. member having the floor to allow a minister of the Crown to put a question, or to give an explanation.

I do this in all kindness. The hon. gentleman stated that contracts for dredging were let without tender. The hon. gentleman is in error. The evidence i3 that they were all let after public advertisement and receipt of tenders, and let to the lowest bidder.
Renewed without tender.
No, they were not renewed without tender.

I accept the statement of the Minister of Public Works. But if I understand the matter it is this, that there was a time when the Minister of Public Works adopted the system of letting contracts without tender; that there came a time subsequently when he adopted the principle of letting contracts by tender; that when he let these contracts without tender the work was done for a certain price, but that after he let the contracts by tender the price went up.
The hon. gentleman has been misinformed.

That is the statement made in my riding, and it was made by members of the Liberal party for the purpose of proving that the system which was in force previously, of this administration letting dredging contracts without tender, worked better than the system now in force of letting contracts by tender. But that only goes to prove our argument and contention that the affairs of this country have got into such a state because of the patronage system adopted by this government that there is not a Conservative probably in the whole Dominion of Canada who owns any interest in dredging or construction companies or in any _ company which has to do with public affairs. They have practically abolished the principle of competition to such an extent that even when contracts are let by public tender there is nobody to tender but the friends of

the administration and there is really no competition. I say to the Minister of Public Works that it is just such a condition that has produced amongst the people of Canada a feeling of distrust and a belief that no man will tender for public works unless he has some political pull with hon. gentlemen occupying the treasury benches. So, I say that it behooves hon. gentlemen opposite to take advantage of every opportunity that is offered to them for the purpose of restoring the confidence of the people which they, by their actions, have displaced during the last twelve years. If there be some little objection made to the principle of allowing tSnderers to be present when tenders are opened, the objections are comparatively insignificant as compared with the benefit to be derived from allowing them to be present. That is the position I take. I do not know that I can say more than that, but I desired to give expression of my emphatic approval of the original motion made by my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid) and to say that it will receive my hearty support and that I have always been in favour of the principle of letting contracts by public tender in a bona fide, upright and conscientious manner.

Mr. Speaker, I have to ask the indulgence of the House while I say a few words in regard to the question before us this evening. I would not have undertaken to say anything had it not been that the question of tender and contract came up in the constituency which I have the honour to represent in this House. Therefore, I feel that I am compelled to say a word on this matter. I was somewhat amused to hear the arguments that were put before us as to why we should not have this motion passed. One of these arguments was that set up by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) in which he said that if we give you three members you will ask for four. I say let us have four if we need them and if four are not enough let us have five ; and if five are not enough let us have six, I say that we will ask for the whole House of Commons if it be necessary in order to have this work done in an honest and business-like way. If we cannot have it properly done in the Department of Public Works, or in any other department, we will then move to have these tenders opened on the table of the House and before every member in order that it may be honestly and properly done. Therefore, I say that it was to my mind a very unreasonable and unfair argument for the Minister of Public Works to make in opposition to the motion of my hon. friend. The question is : Are three better than two ? Is there anything wrong with the third man in these departments or is there any reason why he should not call them in ? What is the matter with Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
him ? What is the reason ? Is he too busy? I am informed that the departments are well equipped with officials ; in fact, all the evidence that we have in the country is to that effect. Have you no confidence in the third man ? If you have confidence in him, what is the reason for saying he should not be there ? Is there any reason why the tenderer should not be there ? . As the Minister of Public Works said we will have to give him notice. Tell him that the tenders will be opened on a certain particular day and if he is not there it will be his fault and not yours. That is the position I take. In the constituency that I have the honour to represent we have had a great deal of difficulty over tenders. It has not been between Conservatives and Liberals but between Liberals and Liberals, because we have Liberals and Liberals in our constituency. What has been the condition ? The hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) knows very well that in that particular constituency we have a gentleman who supplies ham and bacon to the Militia Department there. What is the result ? A good Liberal sent in a tender for those supplies at the same time as the successful tender was sent in, and he proved to the satisfaction of the public at least, whether he proved to the satisfaction of the department or not, that his tender was lower than that of the man who now has the contract. Moreover, the gentleman who put in that tender is now supplying the gentleman who received the contract to supply the department, and if anybody desires the name of this gentleman I will give it to him. I have risen because in the constituency which I have the honour to represent as the junior member this matter has been brought up and dealt with at very great length. Therefore, diffident as I feel about getting up upon this, almost my first day in the House, I could not forego the opportunity of placing myself on record upon the question. To my mind no argument has been presented to convince this House that the resolution of my hon. friend for Grenville (Mr. Reid) should not be adopted. On the contrary, every argument which has been advanced from the other side of the House indicates very strongly to me at least that I should support this motion. We should not treat this as a party question, are we not here representing the people ? Have we not been sent here by the people ? Should we keep any information away from them ? Should we not give them all the information we can ? Should we let them be part and parcel of the government of the country or should we, having got their votes to place us in this parliament, say to them that we do not want to let them know anything more, until perhaps four or five years from now when we may go back to them and again seek their support, in the meantime

forgetting all about them ? Would anybody say to the people in his constituency that he would oppose such a resolution as this ? Would any member Irom any constituency in the Dominion of Canada stand face to face before his electors and say that he would refuse to support any measure that would give information to the people with regard to tenders and contracts ? Would he say :	We are going to award
these contracts as secretly as we possibly can ? He would not dare to say that but he would say : If there is anything wrong, if you think there is any better way in which these contracts can be awarded we will be glad to adopt it and to give to the people all the information that they may require in order to satisfy them as to the manner in which this business is done. We are here for the purpose of dealing with these matters. I do not consider it a party question. It should not be a party question. It is a question that involves the security of the people of Canada.
I was somewhat surprised at the conversational argument which took place between the Minister of Public Works and one hon. gentleman on this side of the House. What was the argument ? To my mind it was an effort to try and persuade those who were listening that something had not happened that had happened, simply by saying:	I
did not say that particular thing at that particular time or date, and I am not going to tell you what I did say or at what particular time I said it; you must guess it. The question was asked why it was that some gentleman in St. John was enabled to secure $35,000 or $36,000 out of the contract for which amount he had performed no service. We in our part of the country have not been informed as to how this was brought about. I do not know how he got this money, whether the contractor put his contract in for fifty cents and was told to increase it to fifty-five, and to give five cents to some one else, the fact remains that some one got $35,000 or $36,000 to which he had no right and for which he has never given a day's work to this country. That is how it appears to me. In the city of Halifax we have had a great deal of the patronage evil, so much so that it is almost a wonder to see my colleague and myself here.
My colleague and I have been returned to this House because the good Liberals of the city of Halifax are beginning to realize that public men in offices of public trust must deal properly with the money of the people of Canada. The people of Halifax believed that iii order to bring about that desired end they could no longer return to parliament the two former members, and they were two very good men in private life; no better men ever came to this House in their capacity as private citizens. But the people of Halifax came to the conclusion that supporting as they did the government of the day in all its transactions, they were useless as members of parliament, and they told them: You must stay at home. Of course, Sir, it may happen that my. constituents will at some future date lose confidence in me, but if they do it will not be because during my career in this House I have not stood up under all circumstances for an economic and honest expenditure of the money of the people. It is not necessary that I should cite as examples contracts that have been awarded in my own city, but let me ask, what better security for square dealing can a minister of the Crown have than that when he calls in his first man and his second man to be present with him, there should also be present the men who have tendered. In what more honest way can the rights of the public be guarded." The Minister of Public Works has told us that the tenderers might conspire to secure a higher price, but cannot the same thing occur to-day .under the present system. Will we be in any worse position in that regard, if the resolution is adopted than we are now. I say no. I say that the collusion between tenderers which the Minister of Public Works seems so much afraid of is far easier of accomplishment to-day than it could possibly be under the system which the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) proposes. I shall support the principle of the resolution before the House, and I shall support it because it is a resolution that the people of my constituency sent me here to support. I take it for granted that there is not a man in this House who can go before any intelligent audience in the Dominion of Canada and defend any other principle than that which is embodied in the resolution which I shall be most happy to vote for.

Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the statement made by the hon. member (Mr. Crosby) that no intelligent man can go before an intelligent audience in this country and defend the principle of the regulation which has been suggested by the Minister of Public Works, I feel that I could go before such an audience and successfully uphold what the hon. minister (Mr. Pugsley) proposes. I represent constituents who are just as intelligent, I think more so, than those represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Crosby), and I would not he at all alarmed to go before my people and defend the regulations passed by the Governor in Council and to-day submitted for our consideration. I therefore have much satisfaction in supporting the amendment of my hon. friend from Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), which I believe meets all the requirements of the case. I am a new member and therefore not acquainted with the procedure of this parlia-

ment, but was under the impression that a discussion such as this was more likely to take place during the last session of a parliament than at the first session of a new parliament. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have heard practically the same kind -of talk as we have heard to-day, on thirty-five public platforms during the last campaign. We had charges brought against the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) and the hon. member for Assiniboia ( Mr. Turriff), but we found in every case that those who made the charges were utterly incapable of proving them. The hon. gentleman from Assiniboia, next to the hon. member for Brandon, was, during the last campaign probably the most abused man in this Dominion. He can have no idea of the manner in which his name was bandied about the country, and if he had had a thousand ears they would all have been burning. But, in every instance where charges were made against that hon. gentleman and against others with reference to the procedure in connection with the opening of tenders, the accusers invariably stopped before they got to the end. We were told that when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Turriff) was in office the tenders for timber limits were opened in the secrecy of a dark room. But those who made the charges never told all that happened; they never told the people that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) waited in the Public Accounts committee room day after day to get a chance to prove the falsity of these charges. They did not tell the people that the Conservatives tried to close up the proceedings in the Public Accounts Committee before the hon. gentleman could have had an opportunity to vindicate his own reputation. When the campaign opened I was not so well informed as to the proceedings in this parliament as I hope to be in the future, but I had with me the report of the Public Accounts Committee and the evidence taken before it, and I was able to show to the people that the hon. member (Mr. Turriff) gave his evidence fairly and squarely before the committee, and that his secretary gave her evidence clearly and well, and that that evidence proved beyond a shadow of doubt that it was false to state that the tenders had been opened in any fraudulent manner whatever. It occurs to me as rather peculiar also that the hon. gentlemen who to-day have addressed the House from the Conservative benches have also neglected any reference to that phase of the question But, Sir, I may say that the people of Prince Edward Island took no stock in the charges which were made, and that Conservatives and Liberals alike came to the conclusion that this was but a repetition of the same old story which they had heard repeated so often by our Conservative friends and that there was no Mr. WARBURTON.
foundation for the charges, and so my colleague and I redeemed our constituency for the Liberal party, and placed it with the other constituencies which have returned members here to work for the good government of Canada. In not a single instance, Sir, did the Conservatives succeed in proving the correctness of any of their charges against any member or supporter of the government or against the government as a whole. These charges of general wrongdoing are very easy to make, but they are not so easy to prove. There was ample opportunity last session, if I read correctly the reports of the Public Accounts Committee, to prove this or any other charge that might be made, and to prove it up to the hilt; and what I am surprised at is that if these charges were so notorious and glaring, they were not then proved up to the hilt.
I listened with much pleasure and satisfaction to the certificate of good character given by the Minister of Railways of the former Conservative governments to the various governments of which he was a member. His statement of the good character of those governments and of every member of them was somewhat of a surprise to me, because it rather clashed with the ideas I had formed of the political history of this country for a good many years. The earliest knowledge I acquired of the political history of Canada after confederation was that during the rule of the Conservative party we were always hearing of something notorious and corrupt, and that redounded to the disgrace of Canada, beginning with the Pacific scandal of 1873, and ending with such performances as that in connection with the Curran bridge.
A good deal of the discussion this afternoon seems to have taken the form of an attack on the Minister of Public Works. It is not necessary for me to say anything in defence of that hon. gentleman, for I know of no man better able to defend himself. But the fact seems to have been overlooked that the matter referred to was brought before the minister's own province of New Brunswick in the shape of an affidavit, and that the gentlemen who made use of that affidavit were compelled to withdraw it, and withdrew it in shame.
To change the date only.

I am aware that it is alleged that there was an error in the date; but in making affidavits which attack the character of a public man, no lawyer has any excuse for making errors even in dates. If any hon. member of this House had been concerned in making that affidavit, and stated that that was an honest mistake, I would be compelled, under the rules of the House, to accept this statement; but when the men in St. John, who made these statements deliberately, and read them before a public meeting,

say that that was an honest mistake, I for one refuse to believe them. However, that matter has been judged by the people of this country. The changes were rung on these charges on every platform throughout the length and breadth of the land, and _ the people of New Brunswick, the province from which the Minister of Public Works comes, gave a decided verdict in his favour, sending him back to this House with a representation of eleven out of thirteen which it seems to me is a remarkably good certificate of character
We have head references to dredging contracts. In the part of the country from which I come I have herd no complaints on that score; the dredging contracts have been carried on satisfactorily, and at no very great expense. I did hear that the Minister of Public Works was badgered in this House last session for extending contracts for dredging purposes which had already been let, and that there was such an outcry that he gave way and called for new tenders, with the result that the new prices were considerably higher than those for which he could have renewed the old contracts, and the Dominion of Canada consequently lost a large sum of money, I think over $100,000 a year.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby), spoke of the good work done in Halifax by the good Liberals and Conservatives of that city. Well, Halifax is a very fine place, but it has had a peculiar record in Dominion politics. Some years ago it was represented by my good friend the late Hon. A. G. Jones; but there seems to be a lack of stability about it, for it frequently changes from one party to the other. It seems to be something like the monster which is always crying for more, more, and looking for something new. It has always been looking to the government to do something more for it, whether building elevators or something else, though it is a very wealthy city. I suppose in doing this it is consulting its own interests. I expect that four years hence it will change its representation back again to the Liberal party, and eight years hence it will perhaps change again. In the county I represent we have also good Liberals and Conservatives. They took the record of the present government into favourable consideration, with the result that they enabled my colleague and myself to bring that county back to what is and should be its natural home, and unless things change very materially, we propose to keep it there.
The hon. members of the opposition seem to be suspicious of everything. I suppose oppositions are born suspicious-it comes natural to them. Our hon. friends opposite are very often suspicious.
