A few months ago they were even suspicious that the country was going to turn out the present government and put them in office. But the
results of the_ general election have shown most conclusively and satisfactorily that that suspicion was absolutely unfounded. I do not propose to take up any more time of the House in discussing this matter. I think it has been fairly well thrashed out, and being a new member I shall not trespass any more, Mr. Speaker, on your attention.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the present debate having hitherto been carried on in the English language, it would not appear amiss that I should add a few words in French.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) stated a moment ago that the principle at stake being one in which everybody must concur, no intelligent man in Canada could reasonably vote against it.
I am well aware that in a large number of Canadian constituencies, this argument was used for the purpose of injuring the Liberal government in public opinion and more particularly of discrediting the administration of the departments of government as regards the awarding of contracts. It must be conceded that, in the majority of constituencies, the people pronounced very clearly upon the issue thus placed be-,them the Conservative candidates. What w'as the principal question submitted to the people during the last general election? Our opponents accused the government of being corrupt and of spreading corruption by awarding contracts, not for the general advantage of Canada, but in the interest of the friends of the Liberal party and to the detriment of the national treasury. Such were the charges made by our opponents. Were those charges substantiated? They were repeated in the constituency where I had the honour of running and the Liberal candidate was returned. When asked: Have you any means of proving the truth of such charges, have they been investigated and with what result? they were constrained to admit that no proof had been adduced, and the people understood the situation. They felt that groundless charges should not be considered. It was sought to create the impression that all public contracts were granted by favour. It was said and repeated that the government could not be acting in the public interest, but that they considered only the return of the Liberal party and the private advantage of their friends.
The resolution now submitted by the member for Grenville is but a continuation of the same policy. It seems to me that the majority in this House should therefore reject it. Our opponents were either right or wrong. The people by their recent, verdict have declared them wrong.
The people having thus given judgment, should we go any further? If, as the hon. member who preceded me remarked, the

investigation had established that contracts were being granted contrary to the interests of Canada, not one member, I am sure, would have opposed the new method now suggested for putting a stop to all further abuses in that respect.	, ,
I have no desire to prolong this aebate, but I consider it my duty to explain why I shall presently vote against the resolution submitted by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Eeid).	T,
It is a question of principle, says lie. It is true. It is a question of principle, more especially as regards ministerial responsibility. It is the minister's duty to award contracts and to do so in the public interest. In such cases the lowest tender is not always the best, and each case should be considered on its merits. Does it not frequently happen that a tenderer is not in a position to properly carry out the contract? The tender may frequently be made by a man who, with the support of a few friends, is entering into an enterprise the nature of which he knows nothing, a man of small experience and perhaps over confident. In such cases should not the minister use his own judgment? Ministerial responsibility comes in here and it is the fundamental principle over our system of government. The responsible minister decides in what manner contracts shall be awarded.
What is the subject of the resolution now submitted to the House? Does it not tend gradually to deprive the ministers of that responsibility? Is it not natural that the head of a department should consider not only the amount of a tender, but also the qualifications of the tenderer? This appears to me to be the true principle that should guide us, the maintenance of ministerial responsibility. If the minister were bound by hard and fast rules, what would become of the principle? The head of a department would become a mere machine, moving in obedience to rigid and inflexible rules. He would be nothing, his initiative would be gone and the system of responsible government would give place to one of independent commissions. That, I believe, would not be going forward, but backward.
I will say no more. In former parliaments, my county of Dorchester was represented by a Conservative, and this fact confirms me in my intention of opposing the resolution. Since 1896, that riding had constantly favoured the Conservative policy, but this time it has returned a supporter of the government, although every argument which has been adduced here to-day was used during the campaign.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I am a new comer in this House and I think it incumbent upon me to say something on the question now submitted. I do not consider it, as have done some of the members who have spoken before me, an attack directed Mr. BOY.
against the government. It is, to my mind, the enunciation of the principle that we should constantly seek more perfect methods in the awarding of public contracts, and I cannot understand why we should oppose such a resolution.
Has it been shown by any of the previous speakers that the resolution is not of a nature to further safeguard public interest in the granting of contracts? It matters little whether the government view this proposal as a reflection upon themselves. That is not the standpoint from which I consider the question. Conditions are never so perfect as to preclude improvement. The object of this proposal is to give further security and thereby fuller satisfaction to the public in connection with the granting of contracts. It has not been contended as yet that, under our present system, public interest is as fully safeguarded as it would be under the system advocated by the member for Grenville, and no argument has been made so far on that point of a nature to induce to vote against the motion, which accordingly I shall support.

Mr. Speaker, what has taken place this afternoon shows that there is some unrest in the country with reference to the awarding of contracts. I think it would be a great misfortune if the amendment proposed by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) should carry. That amendment, as I understand it, states that the regulation which has been laid before the House by the Minister of Public Works forms a sufficient and a complete safeguard of the public interest in regard to the opening of tenders. The fact that there is a great lack of confidence throughout the country in regard to this question should itself warrant very strong measures in regard to the care of tenders for the future, even if it were possible that the measures proposed by the government were under ordinary circumstances sufficient. I do not, however, think that they are sufficient; they fall very short of what they should be.
It has been stated that the precautions which it is proposed to take are just as great as those which are taken in Great Britain. I have some knowledge of the precautions that were taken in some of the departments in Great Britain some years ago and have no reason to suppose that they have been relaxed. In Great Britain they take a great deal more care of the tenders themselves. In the departments of which I have knowledge the tenders are sealed on receipt, by the department itself. The regulations now proposed contain no such provision. After the tender has been sealed in Great Britain it is placed under lock and key, and in some departments it is further safeguarded by the use of duplicate locks with keys in possession of different officers.

I know that in at least one department the tenders were opened in the presence of at last three of the senior officers of the department, and further that in one department it was the custom not to allow the junior clerks to serve too long a term in a position in which the tenders actually passed through their hands, so that every precaution is taken to prevent any possibility of tampering with the tenders. I do not think it will be alleged that these precautions have been taken there because of charges of maladministration in regard to the tenders; they have been taken in order to provide against any possibility of any suspicion being cast, and in order to give confidence to persons putting in tenders for public works or buildings or for the supply of articles to the public authorities in Great Britain.

My hon. friend seems to have a good knowledge of the practice in at least some of the departments in Great Britain. Does he know that the contractors or the public have been invited to be present at the opening of tenders?

Of course I am speaking from recollection, and I was not present when the tenders were opened, but in the particular department of which I have knowledge I do not think the public were invited to be present and I do not think they were present, but I am not quite certain upon that point. Anyway the logical sequence of what I have said is that it is advisable in this country, at least in the present state of public feeling, that we should have every possible safeguard, and I think the government would be making no mistake if they added to the safeguard which they have proposed, and I feel it would be a great pity if the House should adopt the amendment proposed. The proposals of the government are open to criticism. Personally I do not like the idea of having the minister as one of the officers to open the tenders. No doubt in most cases the matter will ultimately have to go to the minister, but the opening of tenders should be left to the senior permanent, non-partisan officials; the presence of the minister is introducing the political side into the detailed workings of the department. I hope the government will not allow the amendment to pass, but will give further consideration to the matter and that the Hoijse will not put itself on record as endorsing a regulation which does not go far enough and does not sufficiently guard the interests of the country.

Mr. Speaker, it is more on account of the spirit of the motion of my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) and of the speeches by which it has been supported than of the motion itself, that I personally refuse to accept it, because I cannot see 8
that it makes any great difference whether one, two or three persons are present when a tender is opened. The motion and the speeches in support of it have been inclined to cast a reflection on the ministers of this government which personally I do not believe is deserved. It has struck me as peculiar in listening to the speeches this afternoon that there should be such an amount of suspicion in the parts of the country from which our Conservative friends come, because this is the first time in my life that I have heard of any suspicion that the tenders were not properly opened or that contracts were not properly awarded by this government. I very well remember a tender for a public building during the time of my friend the late Hon. James Sutherland, when Mr. Sutherland as Minister of Pubic Works went so far as to put up the money for the deposit for one of the tenderers, a friend of his and of mine, at the same time telling him most distinctly that although he was a very strong personal friend of his, and although he thought a great deal of him his tender would have to be the lowest or he would have no chance of getting a contract. It was only ^ this afternoon that I heard that our ministers are so dishonest that the contracts are not properly awarded. I am sure that the suggestion cannot be well founded, that it is entirely a matter of imagination. I have in my private and semi-public life often heard people accused of graft or of having some hidden reason for doing certain things, although I knew personally and absolutely that there was no ground for the charge except the mean suspicion of the mind of the person who originated it.
I can see nothing in the argument that the minister himself should not be one of those present at the opening of tenders, because under the constitution, so far as I have read it, the matter has to go to the minister eventually and he might just as well open the tender as have his secretary or some other subordinate official do so. After the receiving of tenders, the mere sealing and locking up of the document is of little importance, although I have no doubt they are sealed when they are put away. After all it is a matter of trust. If the minister and one of his subordinates wanted to be dishonest, the presence of the minister at the opening of the tenders would not greatly increase their opportunities of doing so. No matter what safeguard we adopt the tenders will have to be sent to some one. Perhaps they might be sent in some conspicuous manner, by a balloon or something of that kind so that every one could see them, but as it is essentially a matter of trust, I do not see what advantage would be gained by that.
What difference does it make whether there are one or two or three of the minister's assistants present at the opening of tenders? If the minister were dishonest he

could keep any wrong-doing as secret with two or three subordinates as with one. But what reason have we to suppose the minister will be dishonest, that he will not do w'hat is absolutely fair? Is it not the privilege of every member on either side of the House to ask the minister what the tenders have been and all particulars?
Hear, hear.

If that is the case, would not the minister be a green fellow and a very innocent fellow who would vary a tender? A man in any part of the country, in my constituency or any other, who tendered for any contract would certainly find out the amounts of the other tenders and if he could not find it out himself, would he not ask some member of this House to find out for him. Now you might say that after the tender is let there is no recourse. But at the same time, is it not asking too much of our credulity to believe that any minister would be so innocent as to confirm a tender that was not the lowest unless he had some very good reason to believe that it was in the public interest to confirm it, especially in view of the fact that he might have to tell this House at any moment what the tender was, and all the particulars concerning it? Looking at all the circumstances surrounding this motion', it seems to me that it has been moved for the sole purpose of casting a reflection on the minister of this government, and for that reason I shall vote for the amendment.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to the remarks of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Nesbitt), and I have only to say that if his theory is carried out to its logical fulfilment, we would do away with all safeguards, and make everything a matter of trust in all the departments of the government, as well as in all corporations, leaving everything as a mere matter of confidence in a person's integrity. I think that would not be a very successful way of conducting departmental business. I do not think my hon. friend the Postmaster General would let it go that way in his large department. My hon. friend from Prince Edward Island seemed to feel as if it were altogether out of place to say anything more in criticism of departmental uprightness and the like of that, because the matter had been brought up in the general elections and the government had been returned to power. Well, that is a rough and ready, hut not the most thorough, vindication of the acts of the government on the ground that they carried a majority of the constituencies.
But I wish to make a little more clear what I am afraid the Minister of Public Works left a little hazy with reference to the McAvity affair. It is important that we should have a proper conception of the facts, so far as we can get them. Now what Mr. NESBITT.
are the facts? If we go by affidavits, and if we place alongside the facts of the affidavit of Mr. Mayes the affidavit of Mr. McAvity, and what he met in Mr. Mayes' affidavit, and what he did not meet that is what he denies and what he practically admits.
Will my hon. friend allow me to ask him a question?

No, I must make my statement now. I have known my hon. friend a long time pretty well, and I know he would like to break in and make a speech of about fifteen minutes every ten minutes of the time which is allowed me, and I do not propose to let him do it. By and by, if I see there is a good opening for my hon. friend, I will let him in. Now there was a man by the name of Mayes, who lived in the city of St. John. Mayes was a contractor, and owned dredging plant and apparatus, or hired dredging plant and apparatus-that was his business. There was a man in the city of St. John by the name of McAvity, who was not a dredger and did not own a dredging plant, and had not up to that time, or since so far as I know, had anything to do as a part owner, or whole owner, or in any other capacity in reference to dredging. But Mr. McAvity was high in the councils of the Liberal party; he was the high chief muck-a-muck in the city of St. John; he was the great head of the patronage distribution in the city of St. John. There was a man in the city of St. John by the name of Wm. Pugsley, at that time Attorney General of the province. Now Mr. Mayes, the dredger and contractor, put in a tender for dredging at the rate, I think, of 50 cents per cubic yard. That tender was not accepted. It is immaterial whether there were other tenders or not. Mr. Mayes went to Mr. Pugsley, who was at that time the Attorney General of the province, and recounted his difficulties. Mr. Pugsley, according to Mr. Mayes' affidavit, told Mr. Mayes to go and talk it over with Mr. McAvity. Well, we can each take what each one wishes as to what was the significance of talking it over with McAvity. Mayes took the advice, according to the affidavit, and talked it over with McAvity. McAvity, who was not a contractor, is not a dredge owner, said to Mayes, I am going to Ottawa, meet me at Ottawa on a certain date. Mayes went to Ottawa, found McAvity there, met him on that same day. McAvity says to Mayes, What are you willing to do this for?-according to the affidavit-and Mayes says, I tendered for it at 50 cents per cubic yard, I can do it for that, and I am willing to take it now for that. McAvity says to Maves: Why not make it 55 cents, and give the other five cents to me? Mayes says to McAvity, What 'will you do? Will you join me in capital in buying a dredge, or hiring a dredge, and help me out in that way? If

you will, we will go in together and share the profits. McAvity said to Mayes, I am not in that business, but if you get the contract you can easily raise the money at the banks. They went to the minister of the department, the minister being the hon. Charles Hyman. Mr. Mayes sat down outside, and McAvity went inside to the holy of holies, or the holiest of the holy, whichever you prefer. After having been in there for a certain time, McAvity came back and said .to Mayes, I want you to go in and see the minister, and explain to him how it would be better to get a contract for 400,000 cubic yards-they had been talking about the expense-and tell him that if you went to the expense of getting large machinery you ought to have a heavy contract in order to make your profits. Mayes agreed, the affidavit- went on, and explained the whole matter thoroughly to Mr. Hyman, and came back. Then Mayes and McAvity talked about the matter, and Mayes said to McAvity: Well, we will think about it, and see about the agreement, and the like of that. McAvity, according to the affidavit, drew out an agreement ready for signature, and said, I have an agreement here, why not sign it now and get the thing arranged? Then the two talked with reference to the part McAvity was to take, and it ended in this, according to the affidavit, that McAvity promised nothing more than that he would use his influence to get a large contract of 400,000, or so, yards, but he would not take part in^ hiring the dredge or in going into the business on the partnership plan. Then, according to the affidavit, Mayes said to McAvity : Well, what is your part in this? Oh, well, said McAvity, write whatever you please, write something and I will sign it. And here is the regular agreement, written by Mr. Mayes and signed by Mr. George McAvity:
And whereas the said George McAvity is to receive moneys out of the performance of the said contract, he agrees and promises to use his influence and endeavours with the Minister of Public Works or office of the government at Ottawa, to increase the number of yards to he dredged at the aforesaid site of contract.
(Sgd.) GEORGE A. McAVlTY.
I am not reading the whole affidavit; that, I think, is about the essence of the affidavit. The hon. Minister of Public Works places a great deal of weight upon the fact that there was a mistake in the affidavit, that it was incorrect.
Will my hon. friend allow me to ask him a question ? Does my hon. friend vouch for that being an affidavit that has been sworn to ?
I suppose I shall have to read it.

That is not the question.
8}
Mr. FOSTER, (reading)
I,	Gershon S. Mayes, of the parish of Lancaster, in the oi-ty and county of St. John, in the province of New Brunswick, contractor, do solemnly declare that on the first day of September, 1905, on the advice of Hon. William Pugsley, who was then Attorney General of the province of New Brunswick and is now Minister of Public Works of Canada, I had a conversation with George McAvity of the city of St. John, in said province, merchant, relative to tenders for dredging which was then to be done in the harbour of St. John by the Publdo Works Department of Canada of which Hon. C. S. Hyman was then minister.
Then continues a recital of the whole matter and finally :
And I make -this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
Declared before me at the city of St. John, in the city and county of St. John, this 12th day of October, A.D. 1908.

A commissioner for taking affidavits to he read in the Supreme Court.
That is all I have to read ; let it be interpreted as it may. But the Minister of Public Works says:	Do you not see there
is an absolute error. On October 15, 1907, said the original document, I received a telephone message from Dr. Pugsley asking me to call in and see him next day. The Minister of Public Works says that is an error. The very evening that the statement is made Mr. Mayes comes out and says :
St. John, October 13, 1908. Hon. Wm. Pugsley,
Minister of Public Works,
St. John, N.B.
I notice by this evening's papers that you comment on my affidavit stating that you obtained $2,000 from .me oil -October 16, 1907. The date should be October- 16, 1905, and the error is entirely a typographical one which I regret and have taken the proper steps to have corrected.
I remain yours, &c.,

It was unfortunate that a mistake should have been made, but we are all mortal and we all make mistakes ; that is, nearly all of us make mistakes and it does not cast a reflection upon Mr. Mayes or derogate one single iota from the real gist of the statement that he made a typographical error, which, as soon as it came to his notice, he immediately made good and gave the right date. Now, Sir, what is the statement ? It is that Mr. McAvity received from Mr. Mayes $35,933 of the public money of Canada. Mayes had tendered to do the work at fifty cents. He came to Ottawa prepared to tender at fifty cents. The man that Mr. William Pugsley had told him to go and

talk it over with met him at Ottawa and said to this man Mayes, according to the affidavit :	Why not make it fifty-five
cents ? The work is not worth more than fifty cents, you can do it for fifty cents, but where do I come in if you only get fifty cents for it ? Make it fifty-five cents, do exactly the same work and no more and let me have the five cents. The addition was made and he got it. Now, Sir, what happens ? Mr. McAvity makes an affidavit. I have it here. Mr. McAvity takes good care, neither in his affidavit nor anywhere else to dispute in any way the fact that he had received five cents additional and that he had put it into his own pocket, but in his affidavit he tries to justify it by saying that he had a good many conferences and a good deal of trouble and bother about it and therefore he felt justified in taking that amount of money. These are the plain facts of the case. It is not true that Mr. William Pugsley was exactly in the same official position in 1905 that he occupied in 1907, but Mr. Gershon Mayes asseverates in the statement he makes that Mr. William Pugsley, the Minister of Public Works, when he came into office, knew that an arrangement of this kind was being carried on between Mayes and McAvity and that he endeavoured in various ways to facilitate McAvity's interest. Now, Mr. William Pugsley, the Minister of Public Works, may deny that and he has a perfect right to the denial, but this vital statement made by Mayes, and the great main truth is that a middleman comes in and takes $35,993 of the people's money for which he made no return of service to the public, it is sworn that he did, it is not denied and it is in- fact admitted. The Minister of Public Works, the guardian of the department, the Minister of Justice, and the Prime Minister himself all know it, and yet when they were asked by a member of parliament representing the people whose money had thus been wrongly taken as to whether they have done anything or intend to do anything what was the minister's answer yesterday ? No action has been taken by the government. Here is the minister's answer:
The government is not aware that it has a claim against the parties referred to for the amount mentioned or any amount. The records of the Department of Public Works show that tenders for the dredging referred to were called for by public advertisement and that the contract was awarded in a regular and proper manner to -the lowest tenderer.
Two, 3 and 4 answered by -the reply to No.
1.
The questions asked in Nos. 2, 3 and 4 are these :
2.	Has the repayment of -this money been demanded?
3.	Does the government propose to take action for the recovery of this money?

4.	Has the government consulted with or taken the opinion of the Department of Justice as to its rights?
These were the questions asked and the minister's reply is that the government is not aware and that the government does not propose to ask anybody to make it aware. What I put up to the Minister of Public Works and the First Minister is that here is $35,900 of the people's money gone astray. If the affidavit is true, if it be true that McAvity has not gainsaid it by affidavit and he has not and would not, if it is true that he has practically acknowledged that he has got it and there is no doubt in the minds of the people generally that he has, what does this government propose to do about it ? It may declare that it has no responsibility, and make no move, but as long as there' is a shred of conscience or an ounce of consistent thinking and of principle in the people of Canada the position will be taken, the position will be forced, and the position will make way for itself that these are not the proper guardians of the people's money.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that a question which simply deals with the best mode of treating public tenders cannot be discussed without dragging in what seem to me to be irrelevant matters, and without making statements which are calculated to draw the House away from the real issue which is involved in the motion and in the amendment before the House. What the amendment proposes to do is to provide for everything which I think has been suggested this afternoon as being really necessary to safeguard the public interest. It has been urged, and properly urged, that it is desirable that when the tenders are received that they shall be under seal; that they shall be addressed to the proper officer of the department, and that when received they shall be placed under lock and key until the time shall come to open them. All that has been provided for by the regulation which has been passed by the Governor in Council and of which the House has been informed. We cannot of course guard in every way against the dishonesty on the part of an official, because if an official should desire to be dishonest he might by some mysterious means have the envelopes opened and after examining the tenders have one substituted for another, but it has never been suggested that this has been done or is likely to be done. The regulation provides that those tenders shall be kept under lock and key; that they shall be kept secret until the time comes for their being opened by the minister and the deputy, or by two of the principal officials of the department in case the minister may happen to be absent. It does seem to me that my hon. friends opposite have not

shown that the public interest can be any better safeguarded by having present when the tenders are opened, three officials of the department instead of the minister and the deputy minister as is provided for in the regulation. The only other question which seems to be involved as a matter of principle in the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) is as to whether or not it is desirable that the contractors who have put in tenders shall all be invited to be present at the opening of the tenders. My hon. friend (Mr. Lake) who dealt with the subject very fairly, stated he had a knowledge of the course which is pursued by the British Government in such matters and he says that so far as he knows it has never been customary in England to have the contractors present at the opening of tenders. I have shown to this House that never since confederation has it been suggested that it was desirable that the contractors should be invited to be present, and never has that course been considered advisable by any provincial government in Canada. I ventured to suggest reasons why such a course should not be followed, and notwithstanding all that has been said by hon. members opposite I affirm that in my opinion no good purpose would be served, but on the contrary that it would give an opportunity to contractors to collude together to withdraw their tenders if they saw fit, and to force the department either to accept a higher tender to the disadvantage of the country, or to reject all the tenders and invite new ones. My hon. friend from North Lanark (Mr. Haggart) told the House that there never had been any wrong-doing or any suggestion of wrongdoing in connection with the Intercolonial Railway when he was a minister. I do not question the accuracy of the statement which the hon. gentleman makes, but I do say that the very .course which was pursued by him is the course which is being P^sued to-day. In the case of all supplies which are required for the Intercolonial railway every opportunity is given to obtain them at the lowest market price; the tenders are opened by responsible officers of the department and if any question arises which requires expert advice that expert advice is obtained. Now, let me ask my hon. friend and I think he will answer with that spirit of fairness which he is always disposed to manifest, let me ask him why he wants that course departed from so far as the Intercolonial is concerned? The hon. gentleman said it is because there is a feeling in the public mind that there is something wrong in the way that tenders are now opened, but let me tell the hon. gentleman that if there is any such suspicion in the public mind it has been created by the disposition on the part of gentlemen opposite to make insinuations
without any evidence to support them, and to make charges of graft and wrong-doing without having the slightest tittle of evidence to support such reckless statements. During the last campaign these insinuations were pressed from every platform in .Canada, and the result of the election shows that the majority of the people believe that this government and the various members of it are endeavouring honestly and conscientiously and to the best of their ability to discharge the important duties they have been called upon to discharge. Now, let me say to my hon. friends opposite, and I say it with all sincerity, that although a great deal has been insinuated against my department, it is open to any member of this House to make a motion for the bringing down of the orders in council awarding contracts for Public Works in this country, and they shall be readily brought down. Since I have been a minister, contracts have been awarded involving the expenditure of a good many millions of dollars, and if a motion is made I am quite willing they shall. all be submitted to the closest scrutiny of this House or of any member of a committee of this House. I have pursued the course followed by my predecessors in office since this government came into power, and public tenders are called for by public advertisement for all works which involve an expenditure of over $5,000, except of course in cases of emergency where there has not been time to call for public tenders, and in these cases the special circumstances must be submitted to His Excellency in Council and must be passed upon. Now, Liberals and Conservatives alike have put in tenders for these works, and when hon. gentlemen opposite say that Conservatives will not tender for Public Works at the present time they are stating that which they have no knowledge of and which the facts will prove to be untrue. Conservative contractors do tender equally with Liberal contractors and if the Conservative contractor happens to put in the lowest tender and if he is a responsible contractor certified to by the officers of my department as capable of carrying out the work, he is given the contract in every instance. If hon. gentlemen desire to have the records brought down they will be able to see that the statement which I now make is true, I believe the same applies all through the departments of government. Hon. gentlemen opposite have given as one reason why the tenderers should be notified to be present when the tenders are opened, that there was no more danger of collusion and no more danger of the withdrawing of tenders than there is at present. But there is this difference. Under the present system the tenderers do not know until the contract is awarded what is the bid of the other tenderers, whereas if they were present they would know. Under

the present system they do not know, unless the other tenderers choose to tell them, and so they cannot say what would be the result of withdrawing their tender and refusing to enter into the contract. But if they knew' that one or two tenders were for small amounts, and others were for larger amounts, it would be the easiest thing in the world for them to collude together.
Does it not strike the minister that they might ask one another and find out after the tenders were in?

That is true, but contractors are not in the habit of asking each other after the tenders are in. They do not know what to do, and it is in the public interest that they should not know what to do, until the lowest tenderer is notified and is invited to enter into the contract. That makes the bargain, and when the contract is once entered into there is the security to the Crown for the performance of the contract.
Now, having dealt thus with the resolution which is before the House, let me refer briefly to some matters which have been brought up by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and by some other gentlemen. I had supposed, Sir, that, with the recollection of what took place in the provinca of New Brunswick in the recent election, my hon. friend from North Toronto would have been the last man to want to refer to the matters which were discussed during that election, and upon which the people, to the best of their ability, passed their judgment and rendered their verdict. The hon. gentleman has referred to what he is pleased to call an affidavit made by Mr. Gershon S. Mayes. Let me ask my hon. friend if he can vouch for the paper from which he has read having been an affidavit and having been actually sworn to or declared to?
Mr. Mayes vouched for it himself.
It was to my hon. friend from North Toronto that I addressed the question.
I have read what I have read, and my hon. friend may take whatever he chooses out of it. After he makes his speech he will get his answer.

My hon. friend declines to answer my question. Let me say that I and others are deeply interested in knowing whether this alieged affidavit was actually sworn to, and, in case it was, we are anxious to know in whose possession it is to-day, so that it may be available for use in the courts of justice. Let me say to you, Sir, that in the citv of St. John during the recent election it was whispered to me that upon a certain night, when a great Conservative meeting was to be held in St.

John, a meeting which was to be graced with the presence of Sir James Whitney, the premier of Ontario, and I think the Hon. Mr. Roblin, the premier of Manitoba, as well as other distinguished gentlemen, a bombshell was to be exploded which would drive me as Minister of Public Works out of public life. Well, I was curious to know what was this bombshell that was to drive me out of public life, because I may say to my hon. friend from North Toronto that though a good many things have been said against me by himself and by gentlemen who have been associated with him, it has always been a sort of protection to me in the public mind that I had many early and pleasant associations with my hon. friend. We happened to have gone from the same county, almost from the same settlement, in one of the country districts of New Brunswick, to the university when we were boys. We went in the same year and entered the same class, and it -was always my pride that I was able to follow my hon. friend, even at some little distance, along the lines of good conduct.
You were safe there.

Yes, and when these charges were made against me from time to time, particularly in the last election, my friends and the people generally would say: ' Oh, well, you can't be so bad as they say you are, because we never thought you would be as good as Mr. Foster, and think of the horrible things they say about him.' Well, Mr. Speaker, you will pardon the digression, but on this occasion I was curious to know what was to be said about me, and I had a friend go to this great meeting and see what was this terrible bombshell that was to be exploded. I found that it was in what purported to be an affidavit or declaration, which was read by the Hon. Mr. Hazen, the premier of New Brunswick, and the leader of the Liberal-Conservative party of that province; and among other things it stated that in the month of October, 1907, after I had become Minister of Public Works, and was charged with the duty of administering the affairs of that department and deciding as to contracts which might or might mot be let by the department, Mr. Gershon S. Mayes, a contractor, had an interview with me or had been interviewed by me, and that I had intimated to him that it would be very desirable for him to have a friend at Ottawa to watch his interests, and that he gave to me at that time, when I was Minister of Public Works, the sum of $2,000. That alleged affidavit, as I have said, was read by Mr. Hazen at this great Conservative meeting, it appeared in the papers the next morning, it was telegraphed that night throughout Canada and I believe appeared in every Conservative paper from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not know what my friends in the

various sections of this country thought; I dc not know what my honoured leader thought; but I know what I thought. I realized that if my leader thought there was a shadow of foundation of truth in that statement, I should not have been able to remain a member of this cabinet for a single day. The charge was made against me by the premier of New Brunswick that in October, 1907, after I had become the Minister of Public Works, charged with protecting the interests of the people of this country, I had been so recreant to my duty that I had received a large sum of money from a contractor who was seeking for business with the department over which I have the honour to preside. Sir, a more infamous charge was never made against a public man. On the following morning I called up the secretary of the Liberal-Conservative Association, Mr. Harrison, before whom the affidavit purported to have been signed; for, as it appeared in the morning paper it did not purport to have been signed by Mr. Mayes. I asked Mr. Harrison about this alleged affidavit and said: ' Surely there must be some mistake about it, because I had no transactions of any kind or description with Mr. Mayes after I ceased to practise my profession in St. John and entered the Dominion parliament.' He said he did not know that there was any mistake about it, but he would look the matter up. Later on I ascertained that the date when I had received moneys from Mr. Mayes, instead of being 1907, should have been 1905, two years before, at a time when I was not a member of parliament, not Minister of Public Works, but was acting as solicitor and counsel for Mr. Mayes in important matters.
It is said that Mr. Mayes corrected the statement he had made, but let me say this, that neither Mr. Hazen, the leader of the Conservative party in New Brunswick, nor, as far as I was able to observe, any leading member of the Conservative party or any leading Conservative newspaper, which had been the means of circulating this vile slander regarding myself and spreading is from the Atlantic to the Pacific -not one of these parties ever took any effective step to correct the mistake they had made, to express regret for it and set me right before the people of Canada, and it remained for me, as best I could, to vindicate myself and make the truth known. But, Mr. Speaker, you know that a lie travels very fast and it takes the truth a long time to overtake it; and throughout this Dominion, there are no doubt many people who, even to the day of the election, believed that I was guilty of the crime charged against me by the leader of the Conservative party in New Brunswick.
Regarding the answer I made to the question of my hon. friend, I do not see
how any other answer could have been given. Assuming the statement he made to-day to be true, what does it prove? All that it proves is that, upon the advice of Mr. McAvity, Mr. Mayes put in a tender at a larger figure than he thought, before he left St. John, he could have tendered to do the work for. The tenders which had been called for previously had been called for a good many weeks before that time and were subject to conditions which Mr. Mayes was not able to comply with. One of the conditions was that parties tendering should have a dredge in Canada at the time of filing the tender with which they could perform the work. What Mr. Mayes wanted Mr. McAvity to do, so I understood, was to endeavour to get that disability removed because there was no suitable dredge in the maritime provinces capable of doing the work, and thus enable him to bring in a dredge from the United States. True, Mr. Mayes came to me as his solicitor, who had been his legal adviser in important matters for a number of years, and asked me could I suggest any business man in the city of St. John with whom he might associate in his dredging operations. I mentioned Mr. McAvity as one of the leading business men in the city of St John.
Hear, hear.

Will those hon. gentlemen who are good enough to applaud my remarks tell me why I should not name Mr. McAvity? Mr. McAvity was then, as he is now, a prominent business man in the city of St. John. More than that, I had known Mr. McAvity as a man whose integrity had never been questioned and with whom it was an advantage for any one to be associated in the carrying on of any undertaking involving financial strength, the exercise of judgment, and qualities of that character. I recommended Mr. Mayes to see Mr. McAvity. I supposed that Mr. McAvity was joining in the undertaking by putting up a part of the capital; but as to what the arrangements were, I never had any knowledge until certain statements were made by Mr. Mayes during the recent election contest in the city of St. John. What do the records show? They show that when the tenders were previously called, there were two or three-two if I remember rightly. One was by Haney & Miller from Toronto at one dollar and thirty-five per cubic yard. The other, that of Mr. Mayes, was for fifty cents per cubic yard.
55 cents.

No, 50 cents; but one of the conditions was that the tenderer must have a dredge in Canada, at the time of filing the tender, prepared to, undertake the work. Mr. Mayes could not comply with that condition. Several weeks

after new tenders were called for; and upon representations made to the then [DOT] Minister of Public Works, and in the exercise of his judgment as minister, being convinced, I presume, that there were no dredges in the maritime provinces capable of doing the work, he omitted that condition and tenders were called for without that stipulation.
Who was then Minister of Public Works?

Mr. Hyman was then the Minister of Public Works and the records of my department show that there were only two tenders sent in-one from Haney and Miller of Toronto, who tendered again, and their tender, if I remember rightly, was at $1.25 per yard; and the other was from G. S. Mayes at 55 cents, being a difference of 70 cents between the two. Let me ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether-even supposing that my hon. friend from North Toronto has any ground for entertaining so poor an opinion of the late Minister of Public Works as to suppose he would inform Mr. McAvity of what was in the other tender-let me ask you whether it is at all likely that such a wide difference would have been left between the two tenders as the very big one of 70 cents per cubic yard?
Did I insinuate anything of that kind?

The hon. gentleman said that it is the duty of the government to proceed against Messrs. McAvity and Mayes for the recovery of the sum of $35,000; and that statement, if based at all, must be based on the allegation that the late Minister of Public Works was in collusion with these gentlemen to defraud the treasury. Let me tell my hon. friend-and I tell him as one who has some little knowledge of law and what any respectable barrister will tell him-unless the late Minister of Public Works was in collusion with these gentlemen to defraud the treasury, the government has no claim against either one of them, because the tender of Mr. Mayes was the lowest and was accepted, being the lowest, by the then Minister of Public Works. No claim could therefore be made by the Crown to-day against Mr. McAvity or Mr. Mayes.
Let me say something further with regard to this matter, and I shall be glad at any time to have it fully discussed. The affair did not end there. This affidavit, or alleged affidavit, which was read at this public meeting, was not all there was to this matter, because, although Mr. Mayes has said in it that he was willing to do the work at 50 cents per cubic yard, it is to my knowledge, as Minister of Public Works, that Mr. Mayes was persistent in his demand that I should increase the contract price to 90 cents per cubic yard. Let Mr. PUGSLEY.
me to say to my hon. friend that the statement I made in the city of St. John during that campaign, after the matter had been referred to-which statement is borne out by the records of the department-was that from time to time after the contract was entered into and after I became minister, Mr. Mayes was persistent in the demand that I should increase the contract price to 90 cents, that being the price he was charging for doing other work. The hon. gentleman says that Mr. Mayes was willing to do the work for 50 cents, yet we find him afterwards contending that it was worth 90 cents; and the principal reason why this attempt was made by Mr. Mayes to destroy me politically was my refusal to yield to the solicitations of himself and Mr. McAvity. I held them to their bargain. They claimed that they were losing money, but I forced them to carry out their contract-and I believe that, under my management of the department, so far as this contract is concerned, the government got good service and value.
At six o'clock the House adjourned.

Thursday, January 28, 1909.
